name: Medroxyprogesterone acetate

lead: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) is a synthetic progestin best known as a contraceptive. For appearance, it is used in feminizing hormone regimens for transgender women and to treat excess body and facial hair (hirsutism), and decreased scalp hair is a listed side effect.

It activates progesterone, androgen and glucocorticoid receptors and suppresses GnRH, which lowers sex hormone levels and shifts the hormone balance behind body shape and hair growth. High-dose injectable MPA has been reported to treat hirsutism; trial data for its appearance uses are limited.

paras: MPA comes as an oral tablet and as an injectable contraceptive (Depo-Provera), prescribed by a clinician. In feminizing therapy it is added to an estrogen-based regimen at a prescriber's discretion. Results on hair or body shape build over months.

The injectable label carries a boxed warning for loss of bone mineral density. Blood clots, menstrual disruption and meningioma have been reported, and large trials of estrogen plus MPA in postmenopausal women found higher rates of breast cancer, coronary disease and stroke. It is prescription-only.

chain: Feminizing changes or reduced hair growth
angle.text: Medroxyprogesterone acetate is used in feminizing hormone therapy and for hirsutism, where progestin activity shifts hormone balance, body shape and hair growth. These are off-label to its contraceptive role, with limited trial data for them.

lead: Medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) is a synthetic progestin sold as Depo-Provera (injectable contraceptive, DMPA) and Provera (oral). It was discovered in 1956 and introduced for medical use in the US in 1959.[1][2]

Its main uses are contraception, menopausal hormone therapy and gynecologic disorders. Appearance-related uses are limited: it is prescribed in feminizing hormone therapy for transgender women, and high-dose DMPA has been reported to treat hirsutism, while decreased scalp hair is a listed side effect.[2]

The injectable label carries a boxed warning for loss of bone mineral density.[3] Large trials of estrogen plus MPA in postmenopausal women found increased risks of breast cancer, coronary disease and stroke.[4][5][6]

paras: MPA is used for contraception, menopausal hormone therapy with estrogen, and for dysmenorrhea, amenorrhea, abnormal uterine bleeding and endometriosis. Other uses include appetite stimulation in cancer patients and treatment of some hormone-dependent cancers.[2]

MPA is included in some feminizing regimens because of its progestogenic and antiandrogenic effects.[2] High-dose DMPA has been reported to help hirsutism, and acne and reduced scalp hair appear among reported side effects.[2]

Common effects include menstrual changes, breast tenderness, headache and weight change.[2] The label warns of bone density loss that may not be fully reversible.[3] Some studies link DMPA to higher venous thromboembolism risk, and long-term use has been associated with meningioma.[2]
MPA activates progesterone, androgen and glucocorticoid receptors, lowers GnRH pulses and suppresses ovulation.[2] Half-life is about 50 days after intramuscular injection.[2]

The Women's Health Initiative randomised trial of estrogen plus progestin (including MPA) found increased breast cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke risks,[4][5][6] and its memory substudy reported increased dementia incidence.[7] The HERS trial found no secondary prevention benefit for coronary disease.[8] No studies found of MPA for muscle, hair or facial aesthetics outside gynecologic and hormonal-care indications.

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use in the US.[2]
FDA adds boxed warning on bone density loss.[2]
